doc.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Family show business, Catskills and backing great singers
summary: Soloff's show-business parents, humor in playing, and what the Catskills taught him; he loves backing Sinatra and Streisand.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: That’s good advice. This first playing up in the Catskills must have developed a good sense of humor.
Your questions are great — the playing in the Catskills?
You say must have developed a sense of humor?

My father was in show business, and my mother was a violinist in Vaudeville. My father was a dancer and a comedian. And my whole family had a great sense of humor, and what’s left of it has. And I always loved the humor that Dizzy had in his playing, Clark [Terry] has a lot of humor in his playing, and to me humor and warmth kind of go together in a way. Louis Armstrong, his playing was real serious, but he would lighten it up with his conversation and his —

Persona, his conversation, his singing. What the Catskills and all that experience did in the various different forms of music is it made me learn how to play these different things and decide what I really wanted to do. Now I really only want to do what I really want to do, at this point, which is basically, more than anything else I like to improvise. I mean there are some exceptional jobs. If somebody calls me to back up a great artist, I’ll jump at the chance, because I can learn from the artist. For example when I played behind Frank Sinatra, I would do that at the drop of a hat anytime I got called. Because I’d be doing, first of all playing the greatest arrangements. And the same thing with Barbra Streisand. You know you listen to their phrasing and try to figure out what it is, what is the thing that makes it go straight into the hearts of people when they sing.
